raw_case_text: A 56-year-old Syrian male immigrant was admitted with fever, shortness of breath, and abdominal pain in the upper right quadrant for two months. His medical history revealed no known comorbidities. Emergency surgical examination did not reveal any rebound, muscular defence in the abdomen. Laboratory test results were as follows: white blood cell count (WBC) 13.000/mm3 and C-reactive protein (CRP) 232 mg/dL tomography showed echinococcosis cyst (CE) 102 x 92 mm at the liver segments 6-7. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a CE-4 type cystic lesion of 106 x 70 mm at the right lobe (Figures 1 and 2). The patient was treated with albendazole (800 mg/day), considering the risk of abscess due to long-term abdominal pain and fever, with metronidazole. However, the patient who admitted to the emergency service the next day with shortness of breath was hospitalized with a diagnosis of pneumonia. In the posteroanterior X-ray examination, a consolidation was observed in the right basal segment of the lung (Figure 3). He was treated with ceftriaxone 2 g/day and clarithromycin 500 mg/day. Oxygen saturation was 97%, arterial blood pressure was 105/65 mmHg, and pulse was 80/min. No rale or rhoncus was determined during the auscultation. We concluded that the rupture of the hydatid cyst was responsible for the clinical condition of the patient and planned drainage of the lung infection with an abdominal incision. As the clinical condition of the patient deteriorated and WBC count gradually increased to 22,700/mm3 and CRP to 314 mg/dl, abdominal cavity was entered with a subcostal incision. A grade 3 hydatid cyst with a solid content and secondary cysts was determined. It was extending to the thoracic cavity through the detachment of the laminar membrane. There was no rupture to the bronchial structures. As the cyst was attached to the diaphragm with a large surface, cystectomy could not be carried out in the liver. Due to the multiple millimetric perforations in the diaphragm, thoracotomy was performed. The cyst was ruptured to the thoracic cavity via diaphragmatic invasion (Figure 4). Cystotomy was also performed to remove the cyst localized in the liver and lung, and millimetric perforations in the diaphragm were primarily repaired. A drainage tube was placed in the abdomen and a thoracic tube was placed in the pleural cavity. The patient was followed in the intensive care unit. During follow-up, his blood chemistry values were as follows: WBC: 28.000/mm3, CRP: 27 mg/dL, and procalcitonin: 3.38 ng/mL. Twelve days after the operation, biliary content was observed in endotracheal aspiration, and bronchopleural fistula was suspected. Therefore, rethoracotomy and lung wedge resection were performed. One week later, the thoracic tube was removed due to complete expansion of the lung and absence of air leakage (Figure 5). Repeated abdominal ultrasound showed that 120 mL of biliary fluid was aspirated by the injection from the debrided cyst in the liver segment 7. The WBC regressed to 7400/mm3 and CRP to 15 mg/dL. The patient was discharged on 15th day. In the histopathological examination, necrotic cuticular membrane pieces and bile in the cyst lumen were detected.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old Syrian male presented with a 2-month history of fever, shortness of breath, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with 2 months of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and dyspnea. After initial outpatient prescription of albendazole and metronidazole for a right hepatic cyst, he returned to the emergency department the next day with worsening dyspnea and pneumonia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Syrian immigrant with no known prior medical comorbidities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, shortness of breath, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: blood pressure 105/65 mmHg, pulse 80/min, SpO2 97%. Abdominal examination showed no rebound tenderness or muscular guarding; chest auscultation revealed no rales or rhonchi.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed WBC 13,000/mm3 and CRP 232 mg/dL, which progressed to WBC 22,700/mm3 and CRP 314 mg/dL (peaking postoperatively at WBC 28,000/mm3, CRP 27 mg/dL, procalcitonin 3.38 ng/mL, and regressing to WBC 7,400/mm3 and CRP 15 mg/dL by discharge). PA chest X-ray showed right basal lung consolidation. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 106 x 70 mm WHO type CE4 cystic lesion in the right hepatic lobe.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT demonstrated a 102 x 92 mm hydatid cyst in hepatic segments VI-VII. Subcostal laparotomy combined with right thoracotomy revealed a grade 3 hepatic hydatid cyst with solid matrix and daughter cysts invading through multiple millimetric diaphragmatic perforations into the right thoracic cavity; hepatic/pulmonary cystotomy and primary diaphragmatic repair were performed, followed on postoperative day 12 by re-thoracotomy and lung wedge resection for a biliobronchial/bronchopleural fistula (biliary content in endotracheal aspirate) and US-guided aspiration of 120 mL of bile from segment VII. Histopathology confirmed necrotic cuticular membrane fragments and bile within the cyst lumen.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Suppurative right hepatic hydatid cyst (segments VI-VII) complicated by transdiaphragmatic thoracic rupture and postoperative bronchobiliary/bronchopleural fistula, confirmed by intraoperative exploration and histopathological identification of necrotic cuticular membranes and bile. Treated with oral albendazole (800 mg/day), IV antibiotics (metronidazole, ceftriaxone, clarithromycin), combined laparotomy/thoracotomy cystotomy and diaphragmatic repair, repeat thoracotomy with pulmonary wedge resection on day 12, and percutaneous biliary aspiration, achieving discharge on postoperative day 15.
